CHAPTER XXXIII. LONA’S NARRATIVE

I lay down by a tree, and one and one or in little groups, the children
left me and climbed to their nests. They were always so tired at night
and so rested in the morning, that they were equally glad to go to sleep
and to get up again. I, although tired also, lay awake: Lona had not bid
me good night, and I was sure she would come.

I had been struck, the moment I saw her again, with her resemblance to
the princess, and could not doubt her the daughter of whom Adam had
told me; but in Lona the dazzling beauty of Lilith was softened by
childlikeness, and deepened by the sense of motherhood. “She is
occupied probably,” I said to myself, “with the child of the woman I met
fleeing!” who, she had already told me, was not half mother enough.

She came at length, sat down beside me, and after a few moments of
silent delight, expressed mainly by stroking my face and hands, began to
tell me everything that had befallen since I went. The moon appeared as
we talked, and now and then, through the leaves, lighted for a quivering
moment her beautiful face--full of thought, and a care whose love
redeemed and glorified it. How such a child should have been born of
such a mother--such a woman of such a princess, was hard to understand;
but then, happily, she had two parents--say rather, three! She drew my
heart by what in me was likest herself, and I loved her as one who, grow
to what perfection she might, could only become the more a child. I knew
now that I loved her when I left her, and that the hope of seeing
her again had been my main comfort. Every word she spoke seemed to go
straight to my heart, and, like the truth itself, make it purer.

She told me that after I left the orchard valley, the giants began to
believe a little more in the actual existence of their neighbours, and
became in consequence more hostile to them. Sometimes the Little
Ones would see them trampling furiously, perceiving or imagining some
indication of their presence, while they indeed stood beside, and
laughed at their foolish rage. By and by, however, their animosity
assumed a more practical shape: they began to destroy the trees on
whose fruit the Little Ones lived. This drove the mother of them all to
meditate counteraction. Setting the sharpest of them to listen at
night, she learned that the giants thought I was hidden somewhere near,
intending, as soon as I recovered my strength, to come in the dark and
kill them sleeping. Thereupon she concluded that the only way to stop
the destruction was to give them ground for believing that they had
abandoned the place. The Little Ones must remove into the forest--beyond
the range of the giants, but within reach of their own trees, which they
must visit by night! The main objection to the plan was, that the forest
had little or no undergrowth to shelter--or conceal them if necessary.

But she reflected that where birds, there the Little Ones could find
habitation. They had eager sympathies with all modes of life, and could
learn of the wildest creatures: why should they not take refuge from the
cold and their enemies in the tree-tops? why not, having lain in the
low brushwood, seek now the lofty foliage? why not build nests where
it would not serve to scoop hollows? All that the birds could do, the
Little Ones could learn--except, indeed, to fly!

She spoke to them on the subject, and they heard with approval. They
could already climb the trees, and they had often watched the birds
building their nests! The trees of the forest, although large, did not
look bad! They went up much nearer the sky than those of the giants,
and spread out their arms--some even stretched them down--as if inviting
them to come and live with them! Perhaps, in the top of the tallest,
they might find that bird that laid the baby-eggs, and sat upon them
till they were ripe, then tumbled them down to let the little ones out!
Yes; they would build sleep-houses in the trees, where no giant would
see them, for never by any chance did one throw back his dull head to
look up! Then the bad giants would be sure they had left the country,
and the Little Ones would gather their own apples and pears and figs and
mesples and peaches when they were asleep!

Thus reasoned the Lovers, and eagerly adopted Lona’s suggestion--with
the result that they were soon as much at home in the tree-tops as the
birds themselves, and that the giants came ere long to the conclusion
that they had frightened them out of the country--whereupon they forgot
their trees, and again almost ceased to believe in the existence of
their small neighbours.

Lona asked me whether I had not observed that many of the children were
grown. I answered I had not, but could readily believe it. She assured
me it was so, but said the certain evidence that their minds too had
grown since their migration upward, had gone far in mitigation of the
alarm the discovery had occasioned her.

In the last of the short twilight, and later when the moon was shining,
they went down to the valley, and gathered fruit enough to serve them
the next day; for the giants never went out in the twilight: that to
them was darkness; and they hated the moon: had they been able, they
would have extinguished her. But soon the Little Ones found that fruit
gathered in the night was not altogether good the next day; so the
question arose whether it would not be better, instead of pretending to
have left the country, to make the bad giants themselves leave it.

They had already, she said, in exploring the forest, made acquaintance
with the animals in it, and with most of them personally. Knowing
therefore how strong as well as wise and docile some of them were, and
how swift as well as manageable many others, they now set themselves
to secure their aid against the giants, and with loving, playful
approaches, had soon made more than friends of most of them, from
the first addressing horse or elephant as Brother or Sister Elephant,
Brother or Sister Horse, until before long they had an individual name
for each. It was some little time longer before they said Brother or
Sister Bear, but that came next, and the other day she had heard one
little fellow cry, “Ah, Sister Serpent!” to a snake that bit him as he
played with it too roughly. Most of them would have nothing to do with a
caterpillar, except watch it through its changes; but when at length it
came from its retirement with wings, all would immediately address it as
Sister Butterfly, congratulating it on its metamorphosis--for which
they used a word that meant something like REPENTANCE--and evidently
regarding it as something sacred.

One moonlit evening, as they were going to gather their fruit, they came
upon a woman seated on the ground with a baby in her lap--the woman
I had met on my way to Bulika. They took her for a giantess that had
stolen one of their babies, for they regarded all babies as their
property. Filled with anger they fell upon her multitudinously, beating
her after a childish, yet sufficiently bewildering fashion. She would
have fled, but a boy threw himself down and held her by the feet.
Recovering her wits, she recognised in her assailants the children whose
hospitality she sought, and at once yielded the baby. Lona appeared, and
carried it away in her bosom.

But while the woman noted that in striking her they were careful not to
hurt the child, the Little Ones noted that, as she surrendered her,
she hugged and kissed her just as they wanted to do, and came to the
conclusion that she must be a giantess of the same kind as the good
giant. The moment Lona had the baby, therefore, they brought the mother
fruit, and began to show her every sort of childish attention.

Now the woman had been in perplexity whither to betake herself, not
daring to go back to the city, because the princess was certain to find
out who had lamed her leopardess: delighted with the friendliness of
the little people, she resolved to remain with them for the present:
she would have no trouble with her infant, and might find some way
of returning to her husband, who was rich in money and gems, and very
seldom unkind to her.

Here I must supplement, partly from conjecture, what Lona told me about
the woman. With the rest of the inhabitants of Bulika, she was aware
of the tradition that the princess lived in terror of the birth of an
infant destined to her destruction. They were all unacquainted, however,
with the frightful means by which she preserved her youth and beauty;
and her deteriorating physical condition requiring a larger use of those
means, they took the apparent increase of her hostility to children for
a sign that she saw her doom approaching. This, although no one dreamed
of any attempt against her, nourished in them hopes of change.

Now arose in the mind of the woman the idea of furthering the fulfilment
of the shadowy prediction, or of using the myth at least for her own
restoration to her husband. For what seemed more probable than that
the fate foretold lay with these very children? They were marvellously
brave, and the Bulikans cowards, in abject terror of animals! If she
could rouse in the Little Ones the ambition of taking the city, then
in the confusion of the attack, she would escape from the little army,
reach her house unrecognised, and there lying hidden, await the result!

Should the children now succeed in expelling the giants, she would
begin at once, while they were yet flushed with victory, to suggest the
loftier aim! By disposition, indeed, they were unfit for warfare; they
hardly ever quarrelled, and never fought; loved every live thing, and
hated either to hurt or to suffer. Still, they were easily influenced,
and could certainly be taught any exercise within their strength!--At
once she set some of the smaller ones throwing stones at a mark; and
soon they were all engrossed with the new game, and growing skilful in
it.

The first practical result was their use of stones in my rescue. While
gathering fruit, they found me asleep, went home, held a council, came
the next day with their elephants and horses, overwhelmed the few
giants watching me, and carried me off. Jubilant over their victory,
the smaller boys were childishly boastful, the bigger boys less
ostentatious, while the girls, although their eyes flashed more, were
not so talkative as usual. The woman of Bulika no doubt felt encouraged.

We talked the greater part of the night, chiefly about the growth of the
children, and what it might indicate. With Lona’s power of recognising
truth I had long been familiar; now I began to be astonished at her
practical wisdom. Probably, had I been more of a child myself, I should
have wondered less.

It was yet far from morning when I became aware of a slight fluttering
and scrambling. I rose on my elbow, and looking about me, saw many
Little Ones descend from their nests. They disappeared, and in a few
moments all was again still.

“What are they doing?” I asked.

“They think,” answered Lona, “that, stupid as they are, the giants
will search the wood, and they are gone to gather stones with which to
receive them. Stones are not plentiful in the forest, and they have to
scatter far to find enow. They will carry them to their nests, and from
the trees attack the giants as they come within reach. Knowing their
habits, they do not expect them before the morning. If they do come, it
will be the opening of a war of expulsion: one or the other people must
go. The result, however, is hardly doubtful. We do not mean to
kill them; indeed, their skulls are so thick that I do not think we
could!--not that killing would do them much harm; they are so little
alive! If one were killed, his giantess would not remember him beyond
three days!”

“Do the children then throw so well that the thing MIGHT happen?” I
asked.

“Wait till you see them!” she answered, with a touch of pride. “--But I
have not yet told you,” she went on, “of a strange thing that happened
the night before last!--We had come home from gathering our fruit, and
were asleep in our nests, when we were roused by the horrid noises
of beasts fighting. The moon was bright, and in a moment our trees
glittered with staring little eyes, watching two huge leopardesses, one
perfectly white, the other covered with black spots, which worried and
tore each other with I do not know how many teeth and claws. To judge by
her back, the spotted creature must have been climbing a tree when the
other sprang upon her. When first I saw them, they were just under my
own tree, rolling over and over each other. I got down on the lowest
branch, and saw them perfectly. The children enjoyed the spectacle,
siding some with this one, some with that, for we had never seen such
beasts before, and thought they were only at play. But by degrees their
roaring and growling almost ceased, and I saw that they were in deadly
earnest, and heartily wished neither might be left able to climb a
tree. But when the children saw the blood pouring from their flanks and
throats, what do you think they did? They scurried down to comfort them,
and gathering in a great crowd about the terrible creatures, began to
pat and stroke them. Then I got down as well, for they were much too
absorbed to heed my calling to them; but before I could reach them, the
white one stopped fighting, and sprang among them with such a hideous
yell that they flew up into the trees like birds. Before I got back into
mine, the wicked beasts were at it again tooth and claw. Then Whitey
had the best of it; Spotty ran away as fast as she could run, and Whitey
came and lay down at the foot of my tree. But in a minute or two she was
up again, and walking about as if she thought Spotty might be lurking
somewhere. I waked often, and every time I looked out, I saw her. In the
morning she went away.”

“I know both the beasts,” I said. “Spotty is a bad beast. She hates the
children, and would kill every one of them. But Whitey loves them. She
ran at them only to frighten them away, lest Spotty should get hold of
any of them. No one needs be afraid of Whitey!”

By this time the Little Ones were coming back, and with much noise, for
they had no care to keep quiet now that they were at open war with the
giants, and laden with good stones. They mounted to their nests again,
though with difficulty because of their burdens, and in a minute were
fast asleep. Lona retired to her tree. I lay where I was, and slept
the better that I thought most likely the white leopardess was still
somewhere in the wood.

I woke soon after the sun, and lay pondering. Two hours passed, and then
in truth the giants began to appear, in straggling companies of three
and four, until I counted over a hundred of them. The children were
still asleep, and to call them would draw the attention of the giants: I
would keep quiet so long as they did not discover me. But by and by one
came blundering upon me, stumbled, fell, and rose again. I thought he
would pass heedless, but he began to search about. I sprang to my feet,
and struck him in the middle of his huge body. The roar he gave roused
the children, and a storm as of hail instantly came on, of which not a
stone struck me, and not one missed the giant. He fell and lay. Others
drew near, and the storm extended, each purblind creature becoming,
as he entered the range of a garrisoned tree, a target for converging
stones. In a short time almost every giant was prostrate, and a jubilant
pæan of bird-song rose from the tops of fifty trees.

Many elephants came hurrying up, and the children descending the trees
like monkeys, in a moment every elephant had three or four of them on
his back, and thus loaded, began to walk over the giants, who lay and
roared. Losing patience at length with their noise, the elephants gave
them a few blows of their trunks, and left them.

Until night the bad giants remained where they had fallen, silent and
motionless. The next morning they had disappeared every one, and the
children saw no more of them. They removed to the other end of the
orchard valley, and never after ventured into the forest.

I lay down with my back against the rough flank of a tree whose bark smelled of rain and resin, and watched the day fold itself away. One by one, and in twos and threes, the children slipped from the grass like mice from a hearth-stone and climbed to their nests. Their bare feet made soft, brief sounds—thup of heel on bole, the faint rasp of fingers on lichen—until each small body was swallowed by leaf and shadow.

They were always like that: spent to the bone at nightfall, and at dawn as if poured newly into themselves. Sleep and waking were for them two doors in one house, both opening easily. I was tired too; my limbs had the dulled ache of healing, and my mouth still held the memory of fear like bitter herb. Yet I lay wakeful. Lona had not told me good night; and I knew, with the quiet certainty a hungry man has of bread that is on its way, that she would come.

When first I saw her again, the likeness struck me as sudden as a scent carried on wind. The princess’s face was there—those lines the moon loved—yet in Lona the dazzling edge was blunted into gentleness, and the beauty deepened as water deepens where it runs slower: with childlikeness, and with a mother’s gravity. She looked young, but not untried. How such a child should have been born of such a mother was hard to take in; and yet, happily, she had two parents—say rather three. Whatever had been broken in the blood had been mended somewhere else.

“She is occupied,” I told myself, listening to the forest’s small night-work—the creak of branch, the far cough of some beast, the whispering insects—“with the child of the woman I met fleeing.” Lona had already said the woman was not half mother enough.

At last Lona came. She sat beside me on the roots, and for a little while said nothing. Her delight was in her hands: she stroked my face and the backs of my fingers as if she were calming a dough that had risen too fast, easing it down into obedience. Her touch had the same certainty a good cook has with fire: she knew where pain would flare if she pressed, and where it would quiet if she held.

Then, as the moon lifted herself and began to look through the leaves, lighting Lona’s face in quivering patches, she began to tell me all that had befallen since I left. The moon made her features now silver, now leaf-shadowed green; thought lay in her brow, and care too—yet love redeemed and glorified even that, as salt turns plain food into something that belongs to a table.

After I left the orchard valley, she said, the giants began to believe a little more in the actual existence of their neighbours. The belief did not soften them; it sharpened them. Sometimes the Little Ones would see the huge brutes trampling furiously, perceiving—or imagining—some sign of their presence, while the children stood close by, unseen and safe, and laughed at the blind rage of it. In time, though, the giants’ spite took on a more useful shape: they began to destroy the trees.

They were not clever in malice, but they were strong. A giant would go at a trunk with his clubbing hands until the bark split and the sap bled. Sometimes they tore down branches heavy with fruit and crushed them underfoot, wasting what they could not eat. The orchard’s smells—apple-sweetness, pear perfume, the faint wine-breath of figs—were trampled into mud. The children lived on that fruit; it was their pantry, their market, their morning. To have it spoiled was like having the language of their hunger erased.

This drove the mother of them all—Lona spoke of her so, with the reverence one gives to an elder who knows seed-times and weather—to meditate counteraction. She set the sharpest of the children to listening at night. They were small, but their ears were keen; they could hear the difference between a squirrel’s scuttle and a wolf’s padding, between a branch complaining and a foot intending. And what they heard was this: the giants thought I was hidden somewhere near, meaning, when my strength returned, to come in the dark and kill them as they slept.

So the mother concluded the only way to stop the destruction was to give the giants ground for thinking the Little Ones had abandoned the place. They must remove into the forest—beyond the range of the giants, but within reach of their own trees, which they could visit by night. The plan’s objection was plain: the forest had little undergrowth to hide them. But she reflected that where birds made homes, the Little Ones could learn to live.

“They have eager sympathies,” Lona said softly, as if repeating a phrase she loved. “They can learn of the wildest creatures. Why not take refuge in the tree-tops? Why not, having lain once in low brushwood, seek now the lofty foliage?”

They had watched birds build. They had climbed trees for play. The forest trees were large, and did not look unkind. They went up nearer the sky than the orchard trees of the giants, and spread their arms—some even bent them down—as if inviting habitation. The children made a story of it at once, as children do: perhaps, in the top of the tallest tree, they might find the bird that laid the baby-eggs, sat on them till they were ripe, and then tumbled them down so the little ones could come out. In their mouths, the tale tasted true; in their minds, it was a promise.

Yes, they would build sleep-houses in the branches, where no giant would see, for never by any chance did a giant throw back his dull head to look up. The giants were people of ground and glare; sky made them squint. Then the bad giants would believe the Little Ones gone, and the children would gather apples and pears and figs and mesples and peaches while the giants slept, storing the orchard’s sweetness as carefully as a thrifty household puts by winter jars.

Thus reasoned the Lovers—for so, Lona said, they called themselves, and it was the most accurate name they had—and they adopted her suggestion eagerly. The result was that they became as much at home in the tree-tops as birds, and the giants, ere long, concluded they had frightened them out of the country. “Did you not observe,” Lona asked, “that many of the children are grown?”

I had not. The change had crept like yeast through dough: silent, patient, and suddenly there. But I could believe it easily.

“It is so,” she said. “And their minds have grown too. That has helped me not to fear it as much as I did.”

In the last of the short twilight—and later, when the moon shone—they would go down to the valley and gather fruit enough to serve for the next day. The giants never went out in twilight: to them it was darkness. They hated the moon; had they been able, they would have extinguished her, as a crude man snuffs a candle because it shows him his own ugliness.

But the children soon found that fruit gathered in the night was not altogether good the next day. It held the night’s chill too long. The cut stems wept and the sweetness dulled; bruised peaches turned faintly bitter by morning, and figs, once opened, lost the clean, green scent that makes them feel like a secret. There is a music to fresh food—crispness is a sound as well as a taste—and by midday that music was muted.

So the question rose among them, like hunger itself: might it not be better, instead of pretending to have left, to make the bad giants leave?

By then, exploring the forest, they had made acquaintance with the animals, and with most of them personally. Lona told it with a sort of quiet amusement: how strong as well as wise and docile some were, how swift and manageable others. The children, with their love-first way of speaking, addressed them at once as Brother or Sister—Brother Elephant, Sister Horse—until before long each creature had an individual name. It took longer before they said Brother Bear, but that too came; and the other day, Lona had heard one little fellow cry, “Ah, Sister Serpent!” to a snake that bit him because he played with it too roughly.

Most of them would have nothing to do with a caterpillar except watch it through its changes; but when at last it came from its retirement with wings, all would address it as Sister Butterfly, congratulating it on its metamorphosis with a word that meant something like repentance—turning, returning, becoming otherwise. They treated it as sacred, as if the smallest creature carried in its body the whole sermon of change, though they could not translate it into any other speech than wonder.

One moonlit evening, as they went to gather fruit, they came upon a woman seated on the ground with a baby in her lap—the woman I had met on my way to Bulika. The children took her for a giantess who had stolen one of their babies; for they regarded all babies as theirs, as naturally as they regarded apples as belonging to the tree until gathered. Filled with anger, they fell upon her in a multitude, beating her in a childish manner that was more confusing than cruel. She would have fled, but a boy threw himself down and held her by the feet.

Then, recovering her wits, she recognised them—the very children whose hospitality she had sought—and at once yielded the baby. Lona appeared and carried the child away in her bosom, as one carries warm bread to keep it from cooling.

The friendliness of the little people delighted her; she resolved to remain with them for the present. She would have no trouble with her infant—no crying to hush alone, no milk to coax when fear had dried her—and perhaps she might find a way back to her husband, who was rich in money and gems, and very seldom unkind.

We talked the greater part of the night, chiefly of the children’s growth and what it might mean. I had long known Lona’s power of recognising truth; now I found myself astonished at her practical wisdom. Perhaps, had I been more of a child, I should have wondered less. Wisdom in that land did not always come by age; sometimes it came by listening—truly listening—to what life said in its own dialects: the crackle of leaf, the hush that warns of an enemy, the way a frightened baby breathes.

It was far from morning when I became aware of a slight fluttering and scrambling. I rose on my elbow. Through the moon-dappled gloom I saw many Little Ones descend from their nests. Their bodies made small noises against bark, like the whisper of a broom on a kitchen floor. They disappeared. In a few minutes all was still again.

“What are they doing?” I asked.

“They think,” Lona answered, “that, stupid as they are, the giants will search the wood. They are gone to gather stones with which to receive them. Stones are not plentiful in the forest, and they must scatter far to find enough. They will carry them to their nests, and from the trees attack as the giants come within reach.”

She spoke as one describing preparations for baking: you must gather fuel, you must fetch water, you must grind. War, in her mouth, sounded like household labour undertaken unwillingly for the sake of the children’s table.

“Knowing their habits, they do not expect them before morning. If they come, it will be the opening of a war of expulsion: one people or the other must go. The result is hardly doubtful.”

“We do not mean to kill them,” she added. “Indeed, their skulls are so thick I do not think we could. Not that killing would do them much harm; they are so little alive. If one were killed, his giantess would not remember him beyond three days.”

“Do the children throw so well that it might happen?” I asked.

“Wait till you see,” she said, and there was in the phrase a touch of mother-pride, like a cook’s satisfaction in a knife well honed. “But I have not yet told you of a strange thing that happened the night before last.”

We had come home from fruit-gathering, she said, and slept in our nests, when horrid noises of beasts fighting roused us. The moon was bright. In a moment our trees glittered with staring little eyes as the children peered down. Two huge leopardesses were below: one perfectly white, the other covered in black spots. At first the children enjoyed the spectacle, taking sides as if it were a game, for they had never seen such beasts and thought they played. But by degrees their roaring and growling almost ceased, and Lona saw they were in deadly earnest. She found herself wishing neither would be left able to climb a tree.

A minute or two later she was up again, walking about as if she suspected the spotted one lurked near. Lona woke often, and every time she looked out, she saw the white leopardess keeping watch. In the morning, she went away.

“I know both the beasts,” I said. “Spotty is a bad beast. She hates the children and would kill every one of them. But Whitey loves them. She ran at them only to frighten them away, lest Spotty should seize one. No one need be afraid of Whitey.”

By this time the Little Ones were returning with their stones. They came with much noise, for they no longer cared to keep quiet now that they counted themselves at open war with the giants. Each carried what he could: round river-stones found in some distant bed, angular fragments prised from roots, hard lumps that would fly true. They mounted to their nests with difficulty under the burdens, like small people hauling sacks of grain up to a loft. Once settled, as if all that labour had been only a kind of prayer, they slept at once.

Lona retired to her tree. I lay where I was and slept the better for thinking the white leopardess might still be somewhere in the wood, a silent guardian in the dark acoustics of branches.

I woke soon after sunrise and lay pondering. The day’s sounds came gradually: a far call, a nearer flutter, the thin crack of a twig under some small foot. Two hours passed. Then, in truth, the giants began to appear.

They came in straggling companies of three and four, until I counted over a hundred—great loutish shapes moving between trunks, making noise enough for a world that had forgotten how to listen. The children were still asleep. To call them would draw the giants’ attention; I kept quiet as long as they did not discover me.

But one came blundering upon me. He stumbled, fell, rose again, and began to search about with his dull eyes and duller mind.

I sprang to my feet and struck him in the middle of his huge body. The roar he gave tore the morning. It roused the children like a bell.

At once a storm—hail made of stone—fell from the trees. Not a single stone struck me; not one missed the giant. He fell and lay.

Others drew near, and the storm extended. Each purblind creature, entering the range of a garrisoned tree, became a target for converging stones. The air clacked and cracked with impacts; the forest took on a harsh, percussive music, and then, as giant after giant went down, the rhythm shifted: the children’s throwing became almost like drumming, a fierce defense played on the skulls of those who would not look up.

In a short time almost every giant was prostrate. Then from the tops of fifty trees rose a jubilant paean of bird-song. The children sang as birds sing after a hawk has passed—sound returning to its proper place, the soundscape cleansed of trampling.

Many elephants came hurrying up at their call. The children descended the trees like monkeys; in a moment every elephant carried three or four of them on his back. Thus loaded, the elephants began to walk over the giants, who lay and roared.

The giants’ noise went on and on—gross complaint without meaning. Losing patience with it, the elephants gave them a few blows with their trunks, not to kill but to silence, as one raps a barrel that will not stop booming. Then they left them.

Until night the bad giants remained where they had fallen, silent and motionless at last, as if the forest itself had swallowed their voices.

In the morning they were gone—every one. The children saw no more of them. They removed to the other end of the orchard valley and never after ventured into the forest.
